title: extcap: Added graceful termination of extcap capture on win32
description:
Graceful termination of extcap means any final packets and the
pcapng "Interface Statistics Block" are no longer lost.

WM_CLOSE is used as graceful termination signal, since there are no
other good options for graceful termination on win32.
Any extcap process which is unable to accept WM_CLOSE will still be
forcefully terminated.

notes.body: Do extcap processes actually create a top level Window and run a Windows message loop?  Maybe consider some other Win32 synchronisation primitive, e.g. a manual reset event that is set by Wireshark when it's time to stop?  Admittedly the latter will require work in the extcaps to check if the event has been signaled.

There is no graceful win32 termination solution which will work with all existing extcap binaries by default.

WM_CLOSE is to my knowledge the closest thing to a standard way of doing it on win32. At least it gives extcap developers a chance to finalize the capture properly if they want to.

It is reasonably common practice for win32 command line tools to have a hidden Window and run a message loop, as a workaround for the lack of other good process termination signals in win32.

Without a graceful termination, it is impossible for extcaps to send the pcapng "Interface statistics Block" to wireshark, since that block needs to be at the very end of the pcapng file.

This block contains rather important information such as number of dropped packets. Displayed under Statistics->Capture File properties in Wireshark:
![wireshark_ISB](/uploads/a3fbfa62e5877bbf1f52d3d66f7098a6/wireshark_ISB.png)

I understand the need for graceful termination, but I'm not sure this will achieve anything with the current extcap binaries shipped with Wireshark.

Have you tested any of those?

No, this does unfortunately not achieve anything with the current extcap binaries that comes with Wireshark. None of them can be gracefully terminated as they are written now.
Nor do they support the pcapng Interface Statistics Block, so it would not make much difference anyway.

I have tested two of the extcaps that comes with wireshark to make sure that they still work normally.

I ran into the need for graceful termination when writing my own extcap binary which does support the Interface Statistics Block.

I'm sympathetic to your needs but I'm somewhat reluctant to merge a change to Wireshark that only works with a custom extcap.

I won't stand in the way if other core devs are OK with this approach though.

It is a bit of a chicken-or-egg problem. :-)

None of the extcaps support the Interface Statistics Block, because it is impossible to support it due to lack of graceful termination in Wireshark.

And graceful termination in Wireshark is only strictly neccessary if there are extcaps with Interface Statistics Block support.

The udpdump extcap has support for graceful termination on Linux.

I could add support for the windows WM_CLOSE termination method to udpdump if you wish. It is just 60 lines of code.

> The udpdump extcap has support for graceful termination on Linux.

(By which you presumably mean "on UN\*X"; `sigaction()`, for example, first showed up, in POSIX 1003.1-1988, in the year when Linus Torvalds entered the University of Helsinki, at least according to his Wikipedia article.)

It "gracefully terminates" by immediately exiting when it receives a signal, by virtue of not catching any signals, and by not having much cleanup to do.  It reduces the amount of cleanup to do by doing an `fflush()` after writing each packet, so the window in which immediate termination will result in an incomplete packet at the end of the pipe is fairly small.

If it were to include code to write an ISB, it would never do so, in its current form.

UN*X udpdump would write an ISB if:

1. A closesocket(sock) call is added in exit_from_loop() to wake up the thread blocking on recvfrom().
2. ISB write is added immediately after the main while-loop in run_listener().
3. Graceful extcap termination on UN\*X is fixed in Wireshark: I think there is a mistake in the order of how things are called. The UN\*X version of Wireshark seems to shut down the pipe before it terminates the the extcap today. A SIGINT should most likely be sent to extcaps in the same place where I send the WM_CLOSE. But I don't have a UN\*X machine to test on so I did not touch the UN\*X parts.
@vonnikon What about Windows extcaps that do not run message loops? Example of such extcap is USBPcap.

Any win32 extcaps without a message loop can not be gracefully terminated.

Just like any UN\*X extcaps without a SIGINT handler can not be gracefully terminated.

They are forcefully terminated instead.

Note that I just pushed a change to udpdump, where I added a message loop to handle graceful termination on win32.
EnumWindows is very heavy, it goes through *every* top level window running on the host.

Yes, it does. It is a bit backwards, but it is the recommended method for gracefully terminating a process in win32.

Looping through 100 window handles or so is actually not that bad. It is only done once when an extcap capture is to be stopped.

added 1 commit
  • 80bfc88a - extcap: Added graceful termination of extcap capture on win32
[Compare with previous version](/wireshark/wireshark/-/merge_requests/2063/diffs?diff_id=143001389&start_sha=ed5063daafcb4eed6965b339a924ccfbfafb73a1)

If this requires code changes in the extcap to work, and there's no way to gracefully terminate extcaps on Windows *without* some mechanism such as this, perhaps we should:

1. come up with a new mechanism for running extcaps;
1. deprecate the existing mechanism, but continue to support it on UN\*Xes.

Unfortunately, at least when running from Wireshark, I think there are UN\*Xes on which there are issues with the existing mechanism as well - if your version of Qt doesn't use the GLib run loop, the mechanism we use to get notified when an extcap exits does *NOT* appear to work.

There is no guarantee that Qt on a UN\*X uses the GLib run loop. It might be likely to do so if you're running with an X11 or Wayland-based window system, but the window system used on the desktop UN\*X with the highest market share *isn't* X11 or Wayland-based - it's running on the machine on which I've typed this, and I've seen some issues when debugging some extcap stuff.

A new mechanism with control pipes, even if the extcap *doesn't* have any parameters that can be changed while the capture is in progress, might work here; "stop capturing" would be one message that the controller (Wireshark/TShark) could send to the extcap, and another control pipe from the extcap *to* the controller could, when it's closed, indicate that the extcap has exited.

I think the control pipe is the way to do graceful shutdown from Wireshark to extcap. The only remaining thing is how Wireshark would determine whether extcap supports graceful shutdown via control pipe.

Why would you need control pipe from extcap to controller to indicate extcap exit? What is wrong with current way it works? Currently randpkt extcap generates finite number of packets and it seems to me that it properly terminates.

If the current way it works depends on any function whose name begins with `g_child_watch` working, I'm not sure it would work correctly in Wireshark on any OS where the GUI doesn't run atop X11 or Wayland, and it might not even be *guaranteed* to work there, as Qt might not even be using the GTK+ run loop there.

On Windows Qt is not using GTK+ main loop. In fact the `extcap_child_watch_cb()` doesn't seem to be called at all. Wireshark notices that the extcap has finished when the pipe is closed - the `sync_pipe_input_cb()` calls `extcap_if_cleanup()`.
Should we call `g_main_context_iteration(NULL, FALSE);` periodically e.g. from a QTimer if the Qt does not use GTK+ main loop? Or would that be too hackish?

Switching from using the standard OS services to a custom API for extcap termination would certainly work just as well. Would be fine by me.

Is anyone willing to actually make this happen? Or is it pie-in-the-sky?

Rethinking the extcap API is unfortunately beyond me.
I can fix this bug in line with what seems to be the current Wireshark approach of using the standard OS services for the extcaps. But there is no way I'll be able to change the entire process API for extcaps like you are talking about. I don't have that kind of experience with this code base.
Since 18e08d04d1f04f027fb2a911abfadb2117f8d10d (!7499) the GLib mainloop is always running on all targets and thus the `g_child_watch` functions work as expected.
Hi, I'm working on !5489. Isn't it what is mentioned by extcap API change?

What about [CTRL_BREAK_EVENT](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/console/generateconsolectrlevent)? Can it be used for graceful termination?

I'm not a windows guy, but my understanding of this and a few more events is that they are send to console applications which mean applications with a window. And extcap is not this case.

If I remember it correctly, it is noted somewhere in dumpcap code because developers tried it already.

From the comment in `capture_cleanup_handler()` it looks like it works just fine:
```
    /* CTRL_C_EVENT is sort of like SIGINT, CTRL_BREAK_EVENT is unique to
       Windows, CTRL_CLOSE_EVENT is sort of like SIGHUP, CTRL_LOGOFF_EVENT
       is also sort of like SIGHUP, and CTRL_SHUTDOWN_EVENT is sort of
       like SIGTERM at least when the machine's shutting down.

       For now, if we're running as a command rather than a capture child,
       we handle all but CTRL_LOGOFF_EVENT as indications that we should
       clean up and quit, just as we handle SIGINT, SIGHUP, and SIGTERM
       in that way on UN*X.

       If we're not running as a capture child, we might be running as
       a service; ignore CTRL_LOGOFF_EVENT, so we keep running after the
       user logs out.  (XXX - can we explicitly check whether we're
       running as a service?) */
```

But I think you meant the comment in `sync_pipe_kill()`:
```
        /* Remark: This is not the preferred method of closing a process!
         * the clean way would be getting the process id of the child process,
         * then getting window handle hWnd of that process (using EnumChildWindows),
         * and then do a SendMessage(hWnd, WM_CLOSE, 0, 0)
         *
         * Unfortunately, I don't know how to get the process id from the
         * handle.  OpenProcess will get an handle (not a window handle)
         * from the process ID; it will not get a window handle from the
         * process ID.  (How could it?  A process can have more than one
         * window.  For that matter, a process might have *no* windows,
         * as a process running dumpcap, the normal child process program,
         * probably does.)
         *
         * Hint: GenerateConsoleCtrlEvent() will only work if both processes are
         * running in the same console; that's not necessarily the case for
         * us, as we might not be running in a console.
         * And this also will require to have the process id.
         */
        TerminateProcess((HANDLE) (fork_child), 0);
```

But when sending `CTRL_BREAK_EVENT` with `GenerateConsoleCtrlEvent()` it is possible to specify the process group in `dwProcessGroupId` parameter. But the way it is described is confusing
> Only those processes in the group that share the same console as the calling process receive the signal. In other words, if a process in the group creates a new console, that process does not receive the signal, nor do its descendants.

If the process shares the console unless it create a new one, then the `CTRL_BREAK_EVENT` could work.
This should probably be done via a common API in extcap_base.[ch]. I don't object to merging this as-is for the time being, however.

This is loop of blocking waits and in worst case will freeze the UI for the STOP_SLEEP_TIME. Instead of the loop, it is possible `WaitForSingleObject()` on extcap handle with a timeout.

However, the wait should not be handled in this way at all. Since !7673 there is extcap terminate timeout (does not block UI). It is not yet suitable for graceful shutdown, as dumpcap stops first before `extcap_if_cleanup()` sends `SIGTERM` (on Windows it just terminates the process for the time being due to lack of better solution), but it is one of the many steps needed before the graceful termination can be implemented without hacks.
